claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Liégeois et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Changes in the dynamics of functional networks have been shown to be predictive of disease.
claims.source: Changes in the dynamics of functional networks have also been shown to be predictive of behavioral traits (Liégeois et al., 2019) and disease (Sitnikova et al., 2018; Du et al., 2018; Van Schependom et al., 2019; Salvan et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Sitnikova et al., 2018; Du et al., 2018; Van Schependom et al., 2019; Salvan et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020.

claims.claim: A three-state TDE-HMM can identify oscillatory bursts in a data-driven fashion without requiring pre-specification of frequency, amplitude threshold, or duration.
claims.source: Instead of a conventional burst detection method, we use a three state TDE-HMM to identify bursts in a data-driven fashion.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in the burst detection results (Section 2.1) where the TDE-HMM identifies bursts without pre-specified parameters.

claims.claim: Oscillatory bursts identified by the TDE-HMM have lifetimes ranging from a hundred to several hundred milliseconds.
claims.source: We can see from Figure 1BIV that these bursts have a variety of lifetimes ranging from a hundred to several hundred milliseconds.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 1BIV and stated in the text.

claims.claim: The AE-HMM identifies plausible functional networks including a default mode network, two visual networks, frontotemporal networks, and a sensorimotor network.
claims.source: We see the AE-HMM identifies plausible functional networks (Buckner et al., 2011) with fast dynamics, typically with lifetimes of around 50 ms (Figure 2AIII). We identify a default mode network (state 1); two visual networks (states 2 and 6); a frontotemporal networks (states 3 and 7); and a sensorimotor network (state 4).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 2AI and described in the text, with citation to Buckner et al., 2011 for plausibility.

claims.claim: The functional networks identified by the AE-HMM have fast dynamics with lifetimes of around 50 ms.
claims.source: We see the AE-HMM identifies plausible functional networks (Buckner et al., 2011) with fast dynamics, typically with lifetimes of around 50 ms (Figure 2AIII).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 2AIII and stated in the text.

claims.claim: Visual networks show significant activation (p<0.05) between 50-100 ms after presentation of visual stimuli in the Elekta task MEG dataset.
claims.source: We observe a significant increase (p<0.05) in the activation of the visual networks (states 2 and 6) between 50–100 ms after the presentation of the visual stimuli as expected.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 2BI with statistical testing.

claims.claim: A frontotemporal network shows significant activation (p<0.05) 300-900 ms after visual stimuli presentation.
claims.source: We also observe a significant activation (p<0.05) of the frontotemporal network (state 7) 300–900 ms after the visual stimuli as well as a deactivation of the visual networks (states 2 and 6).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 2BI with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The TDE-HMM identifies networks with distinct spectral (oscillatory) activity.
claims.source: We can see from the state PSDs (Figure 3AI, bottom) that the networks identified by the TDE-HMM exhibit distinct spectral (oscillatory) activity.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 3AI bottom panel.

claims.claim: The TDE-HMM power maps show the same spatial patterns as the AE-HMM amplitude maps for high-power networks.
claims.source: For the high-power networks (states 1–4), we see the same spatial patterns in TDE-HMM power maps (Figure 3AI, top) and AE-HMM amplitude maps (Figure 2AI).
claims.evidence: Comparison between Figure 3AI and Figure 2AI.

claims.claim: The TDE-HMM networks have fast dynamics with lifetimes of around 50 ms.
claims.source: The TDE-HMM networks also have fast dynamics (Figure 3AIII) with lifetimes of around 50 ms.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 3AIII.

claims.claim: Similar networks are observed in rest and task MEG data.
claims.source: We observe similar networks in rest (Figure 4A) as in task (Figure 3A), which is a known result from fMRI studies (Smith et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Comparison between Figure 4A and Figure 3A, with citation to Smith et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Regions with high power activations have high connectivity (coherence) in the TDE-HMM networks.
claims.source: We observe regions with high power activations have high connectivity (coherence).
claims.evidence: Observed in Figures 3AI and 4AI showing coherence networks.

claims.claim: The fractional occupancy of the sensorimotor network (state 4) is significantly increased (p<0.05) in older participants (34-60 years) compared to younger participants (18-34 years).
claims.source: We see the fractional occupancy and switching rate of the sensorimotor network (state 4) is increased in the older group (p<0.05).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4BI with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The switching rate of the sensorimotor network (state 4) is significantly increased (p<0.05) in older participants compared to younger participants.
claims.source: We see the fractional occupancy and switching rate of the sensorimotor network (state 4) is increased in the older group (p<0.05).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4BI with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The mean lifetime of the visual network (state 6) is significantly decreased (p<0.05) in older participants compared to younger participants.
claims.source: The mean lifetime of the visual network (state 6) is also decreased in the older group (p<0.05).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4BI with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The older group has a wider distribution of mean intervals (p<0.05) for the default mode network (state 1) and suppressed state (8).
claims.source: The older group also has a wider distribution of mean intervals for the default mode network (state 1) and suppressed state (8) (p<0.05).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4BI with statistical testing.

claims.claim: DyNeMo identifies more localized power activations and cleaner network structure than the TDE-HMM.
claims.source: We can see from the power maps and coherence networks (Figure 5AI) that DyNeMo identifies much more localized power activations and a cleaner network structure than was seen with the TDE-HMM.
claims.evidence: Comparison between Figure 5AI and Figure 4AI.

claims.claim: DyNeMo networks exhibit distinct spectral characteristics.
claims.source: We can see from the PSDs (Figure 5AI, bottom) that these networks also exhibit distinct spectral characteristics.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5AI bottom panel.

claims.claim: DyNeMo describes brain activity as overlapping networks that dynamically vary in mixing ratios.
claims.source: From the (renormalized) mode time course (Figure 5AII) we see the description provided by DyNeMo is that of overlapping networks that dynamically vary in mixing ratios.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5AII and described in the text.

claims.claim: Modes with activity in neighboring regions show more co-activation in DyNeMo.
claims.source: We observe modes with activity in neighboring regions show more co-activation.
claims.evidence: Observed in Figure 5AIII showing mode correlations.

claims.claim: DyNeMo shows an increased mode contribution (p<0.01) for the sensorimotor network (mode 4) in older participants compared to younger participants.
claims.source: We can see an increased mode contribution (mean renormalized mode time course) for the sensorimotor network (mode 4), which reflects the increase in fractional occupancy we saw in the TDE-HMM (Figure 4BI). We see DyNeMo is able to reveal a stronger effect size with a p<0.01 compared to the TDE-HMM, which had a p<0.05.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5BI with statistical testing.

claims.claim: DyNeMo shows a decrease in variability (p<0.01) for the left temporal network (mode 5) in older participants compared to younger participants.
claims.source: DyNeMo also shows a decrease in the variability (standard deviation of the renormalized mode time course) for the left temporal network (mode 5, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5BI with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The TDE-HMM is less sensitive to amplitude and better able to identify low-amplitude oscillatory bursts compared to conventional amplitude thresholding methods.
claims.source: In contrast, the TDE-HMM is less sensitive to the amplitude (it is better able to identify low-amplitude oscillatory bursts) and can identify the frequency of oscillations automatically.
claims.evidence: Discussed in the context of burst detection advantages.

claims.claim: The TDE-HMM can identify the frequency of oscillations automatically without pre-specification.
claims.source: In contrast, the TDE-HMM is less sensitive to the amplitude (it is better able to identify low-amplitude oscillatory bursts) and can identify the frequency of oscillations automatically.
claims.evidence: Discussed in the context of burst detection advantages.

claims.claim: The TDE-HMM can model dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization whereas the AE-HMM can only model dynamics in amplitude.
claims.source: The TDE-HMM approach is able to model dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization whereas the AE-HMM can only model dynamics in amplitude.
claims.evidence: Stated as a comparison between the two methods.

claims.claim: The HMM assumes mutually exclusive network states.
claims.source: The HMM assumes that there are mutually exclusive network states, whereas DyNeMo assumes the network modes are mixed differently at each time point.
claims.evidence: Stated as a fundamental difference between HMM and DyNeMo.

claims.claim: DyNeMo assumes network modes are mixed differently at each time point.
claims.source: The HMM assumes that there are mutually exclusive network states, whereas DyNeMo assumes the network modes are mixed differently at each time point.
claims.evidence: Stated as a fundamental difference between HMM and DyNeMo.

claims.claim: DyNeMo uses richer temporal regularization through a deep recurrent network compared to the HMM.
claims.source: DyNeMo does have the additional advantage of using a richer temporal regularisation through the use of a deep recurrent network. This has been shown to capture longer-range temporal structure than the HMM (Gohil et al., 2022), and exploring the cognitive importance of long-range temporal structure is an interesting area of future investigation (van Es, 2023).
claims.evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claims.claim: DyNeMo has been shown to capture longer-range temporal structure than the HMM.
claims.source: This has been shown to capture longer-range temporal structure than the HMM (Gohil et al., 2022), and exploring the cognitive importance of long-range temporal structure is an interesting area of future investigation (van Es, 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claims.claim: osl-dynamics is an open-source package written in Python.
claims.source: We present a new toolbox for studying time series data: osl-dynamics. This is an open-source package written in Python.
claims.evidence: Stated in the Conclusions section.

claims.claim: Using Python avoids the need for a paid license.
claims.source: We believe the availability of this package in Python improves the accessibility of these tools, in particular for non-technical users. Additionally, it avoids the need for a paid license.
claims.evidence: Stated as an advantage of using Python.

claims.claim: Using Python enables osl-dynamics to take advantage of modern deep learning libraries, particularly TensorFlow.
claims.source: Using Python also enables us to take advantage of modern deep learning libraries (in particular TensorFlow, 2023) which enables us to scale these methods to very large datasets, something that is currently not possible with existing toolboxes.
claims.evidence: Stated as an advantage with citation to TensorFlow, 2023.

claims.claim: The sliding window approach for calculating time series properties suffers from a tradeoff between temporal precision of dynamics and accurate estimation of properties.
claims.source: However, this approach only utilizes a short window around the time point of interest and suffers from a tradeoff between the temporal precision of dynamics and an accurate estimation of the properties (via a sufficiently large window).
claims.evidence: Stated as a limitation of the sliding window approach.

claims.claim: The sliding window approach is inadequate for studying fast changes in functional connectivity.
claims.source: In Liuzzi et al., 2019, it was shown that this approach is inadequate for studying fast changes in functional connectivity.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Liuzzi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Generative models can identify non-contiguous segments of time series that share the same latent variable, leading to more robust estimates of local properties.
claims.source: In doing this, the model can identify non-contiguous segments of the time series that share the same latent variable. Pooling this information leads to more robust estimates of the local properties of the data.
claims.evidence: Stated as an advantage of the generative model approach.

claims.claim: The HMM uses variational Bayesian inference to learn the most likely state to have generated the observed data.
claims.source: osl-dynamics uses variational Bayesian inference Bishop and Nasrabadi, 2006 to learn the most likely state to have generated the observed data.
claims.evidence: Stated in the description of the HMM with citation to Bishop and Nasrabadi, 2006.

claims.claim: Variational Bayesian inference has the advantage of being able to account for uncertainty in the latent state.
claims.source: This has the advantage of being able to account for uncertainty in the latent state.
claims.evidence: Stated as an advantage of variational Bayesian inference.

claims.claim: The HMM has been successfully used to study dynamics in neuroimaging data in a variety of settings.
claims.source: The HMM has been successfully used to study dynamics in neuroimaging data in a variety of settings (Seedat et al., 2020; Khawaldeh et al., 2022; Vidaurre et al., 2018b; Quinn et al., 2018; Higgins et al., 2021; Sitnikova et al., 2018; Van Schependom et al., 2019; Vidaurre et al., 2016; Vidaurre et al., 2018a; Vidaurre et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: DyNeMo overcomes two key limitations of the HMM: mutually exclusive states and limited memory.
claims.source: DyNeMo is a recently proposed model that overcomes two key limitations of the HMM: the mutually exclusive states and limited memory (Gohil et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claims.claim: DyNeMo uses amortized variational Bayesian inference to learn the most likely latent vector to have generated the observed data.
claims.source: osl-dynamics uses amortized variational Bayesian inference Kingma and Welling, 2013 to learn the most likely latent vector to have generated the observed data.
claims.evidence: Stated in the description of DyNeMo with citation to Kingma and Welling, 2013.

claims.claim: Amortized variational Bayesian inference is a highly efficient inference scheme that is scalable to large datasets.
claims.source: This is a highly efficient inference scheme that is scalable to large datasets.
claims.evidence: Stated as an advantage of amortized variational Bayesian inference.

claims.claim: Time-delay embedding augments the time series with extra channels containing time-lagged versions of the original channels.
claims.source: This augments the time series with extra channels containing time-lagged versions of the original channels.
claims.evidence: Stated in the description of TDE.

claims.claim: Time-delay embedding embeds the autocorrelation function of the original data into the covariance matrix of the TDE data.
claims.source: By adding extra channels, we embed the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the original data (as well as the cross-correlation function) into the covariance matrix of the TDE data.
claims.evidence: Stated in the description of TDE and illustrated in Figure 9CII.

claims.claim: Using TDE data makes the covariance matrix sensitive to the frequency of oscillations in the original data.
claims.source: By using TDE data we make the covariance matrix sensitive to the frequency of oscillations in the original data.
claims.evidence: Stated in the description of TDE.

claims.claim: Training on TDE data allows study of dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization between channels.
claims.source: Training on TDE data allows us to study dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization between channels.
claims.evidence: Stated as the purpose of using TDE data.

claims.claim: The HMM and DyNeMo are trained by minimizing the variational free energy cost function.
claims.source: The HMM and DyNeMo are trained by minimizing a cost function (in osl-dynamics, we use the variational free energy Rezek and Roberts, 2005; Gohil et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Stated in the description of training with citations to Rezek and Roberts, 2005; Gohil et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The HMM and DyNeMo training can converge to different explanations of the data due to local optimum issues.
claims.source: As is typical, this approach suffers from a local optimum issue, where the model can converge to different explanations (latent descriptions) of the data during training.
claims.evidence: Stated as a limitation of the training approach.

claims.claim: A strategy for dealing with run-to-run variability is to train multiple models and analyze only the model with the lowest variational free energy.
claims.source: A strategy for dealing with this that has worked well in the past is to train multiple models from scratch (each model is referred to as a run) and only the model with the lowest variational free energy is analyzed.
claims.evidence: Stated as a strategy used in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The best run from a set of 10 consistently finds the same set of model parameters.
claims.source: Empirically, we find picking the best run from a set of 10 consistently finds the same set of model parameters.
claims.evidence: Stated as an empirical finding.

claims.claim: The age-related differences observed in the young vs old comparison are consistent with existing studies.
claims.source: The age-related differences we observe here are consistent with existing studies (Coquelet et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Coquelet et al., 2020.

claims.claim: An increase in static power could be due to more frequent activations of a particular network.
claims.source: The static (time-averaged) differences we see in young vs old participants can arise in many ways from the underlying dynamics of resting-state networks (Figures 4AI and 5AI). For example, an increase in static power could be due to more frequent activations of a particular network.
claims.evidence: Stated as a possible explanation for static differences.

claims.claim: Static differences in power may arise from altered power within a network while the dynamics of the networks remain unaffected.
claims.source: Conversely, the dynamics of the networks may be unaffected and the power within a network could be altered.
claims.evidence: Stated as an alternative explanation for static differences.

claims.claim: The HMM's stronger assumption of mutually exclusive states simplifies the decomposition and can make interpreting network dynamics more straightforward.
claims.source: While DyNeMo's assumption is arguably more realistic, the HMM's stronger assumption has the benefit of simplifying the decomposition, which can make interpreting the network dynamics more straightforward.
claims.evidence: Stated as a comparison between HMM and DyNeMo.

claims.claim: The HMM and DyNeMo provide complementary descriptions of network dynamics.
claims.source: In short, the HMM and DyNeMo provide complementary descriptions of network dynamics, with either one being potentially useful depending on the context (Gohil et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claims.claim: A better performance in a downstream task indicates a more useful model.
claims.source: It is possible to quantify which model is better using a downstream task. In this manuscript, the downstream tasks are the evoked network response and young vs old group differences. We argue a better performance in the downstream task indicates a more useful model.
claims.evidence: Stated as a criterion for model evaluation.

claims.claim: osl-dynamics can compute static network descriptions using the same methodology as state or mode specific network estimation in dynamic approaches.
claims.source: osl-dynamics can also be used to compute static network descriptions, including conventional static functional connectivity. This uses the same methodology as the state (or mode) specific network estimation in the dynamic approaches, making comparisons between dynamic and static perspectives more straightforward.
claims.evidence: Stated as a feature of the toolbox.

claims.claim: The HMM has been validated on simulated data for burst detection applications.
claims.source: Both the HMM and DyNeMo have been validated on simulated data for each application. See Quinn et al., 2019 for a demonstration of the HMM's ability to identify oscillatory bursts and Vidaurre et al., 2016; Gohil et al., 2022 for a demonstration of the HMM/DyNeMo's ability to identify dynamic networks.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Quinn et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The HMM and DyNeMo have been validated on simulated data for identifying dynamic networks.
claims.source: Both the HMM and DyNeMo have been validated on simulated data for each application. See Quinn et al., 2019 for a demonstration of the HMM's ability to identify oscillatory bursts and Vidaurre et al., 2016; Gohil et al., 2022 for a demonstration of the HMM/DyNeMo's ability to identify dynamic networks.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Vidaurre et al., 2016; Gohil et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The burst detection approach assumes bursting is being looked for in a single channel (brain region) at a time.
claims.source: This approach assumes that we are looking for bursting in a single channel (brain region) at a time; separate HMMs can be used to detect bursting in each channel.
claims.evidence: Stated as an assumption of the burst detection approach.

claims.claim: The multitaper approach is used to calculate PSDs due to its ability to accurately estimate spectra.
claims.source: We use the multitaper approach described in Vidaurre et al., 2016 to do this due to its ability to accurately estimate spectra.
claims.evidence: Stated with citation to Vidaurre et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Principal component analysis is often needed after TDE for dimensionality reduction to ensure data fits into computer memory.
claims.source: This means after TDE we have a very large number of channels (number of embeddings times the number of regions). Therefore, we often need to perform principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction to ensure the data fits into computer memory.
claims.evidence: Stated as a practical necessity in the TDE-HMM pipeline.

claims.claim: Non-negative matrix factorization is applied to stacked subject and state-specific coherence spectra to identify common frequency bands of coherent activity.
claims.source: Note that we also use the spectral decomposition approach introduced in Vidaurre et al., 2018b to specify a frequency range for calculating power maps and coherence networks. This involves applying non-negative matrix factorization to the stacked subject and state-specific coherence spectra to identify common frequency bands of coherent activity.
claims.evidence: Stated with citation to Vidaurre et al., 2018b.

claims.claim: The GLM-based approach is used to calculate mode and region-specific PSDs in DyNeMo by regressing mixing coefficients onto a cross spectrogram.
claims.source: To calculate mode and region-specific PSDs, we use the approach based on the General Linear Model (GLM) proposed in Quinn et al., 2022a where we regress the mixing coefficients onto a (cross) spectrogram, see Gohil et al., 2022 for further details.
claims.evidence: Stated with citations to Quinn et al., 2022a and Gohil et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The mode time course in DyNeMo does not contain information regarding the relative magnitude of each mode covariance.
claims.source: Note that an additional complication related to the mode time course is that it does not contain any information regarding the relative magnitude of each mode covariance.
claims.evidence: Stated as a complication in interpreting DyNeMo results.

claims.claim: The mode time course is renormalized by weighing each mode time course by the trace of its mode covariance.
claims.source: We account for this by renormalizing the mode time course (We weigh each mode time course by the trace of its mode covariance and divide by the sum over modes at each time point to ensure the renormalized mode time course sums to one), this is discussed further in Gohil et al., 2022.
claims.evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claims.claim: A two-component Gaussian Mixture Model can be used to binarise DyNeMo mode time courses to calculate HMM-like summary statistics.
claims.source: Alternatively, if we were interested in calculating the same summary statistics as the HMM (fractional occupancy, lifetime, interval, switching rate) we would first need to binarise the mode time courses. This can be done using a two-component Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), which is discussed in Gohil et al., 2022.
claims.evidence: Stated with citation to Gohil et al., 2022.

claims.claim: A two-component GMM is used to threshold networks by fitting to the distribution of connections, with one component representing background connections and the other representing atypically strong connections.
claims.source: In this work, we will specify the threshold using a data-driven approach where we fit a two-component GMM to the distribution of connections in each network. We interpret one of the components as the distribution for background connections and the other as the distribution for atypically strong connections, which is what we display in each plot.
claims.evidence: Stated as the thresholding method used.

claims.claim: For static networks, the top 5% of connections are displayed rather than using the GMM thresholding approach.
claims.source: Note, for the static networks we select the top 5% of connections to display in each plot rather than the GMM approach we used to threshold the dynamic functional networks.
claims.evidence: Stated as the thresholding method for static networks.

claims.claim: Different state/mode time courses can lead to similar values for the variational free energy.
claims.source: As is typical, this approach suffers from a local optimum issue, where the model can converge to different explanations (latent descriptions) of the data during training. That is, different state/mode time courses can lead to similar values for the variational free energy.
claims.evidence: Stated as a characteristic of the training process.

claims.claim: The final description from HMM/DyNeMo training can be sensitive to the stochasticity in updating model parameters and the initial parameter values.
claims.source: The final description can be sensitive to the stochasticity in updating model parameters and the initial parameter values.
claims.evidence: Stated as a source of variability in training.

claims.claim: Results are deemed reproducible if the same model parameters are consistently inferred from a dataset.
claims.source: We deem a set of results as reproducible if we are consistently able to infer the same model parameters from a dataset.
claims.evidence: Stated as the criterion for reproducibility.

claims.claim: For a given set of hyperparameters, only the relative difference between values for the variational free energy is important.
claims.source: Note, for a given set of hyperparameters, only the relative difference between values for the variational free energy is important.
claims.evidence: Stated as a note about interpreting variational free energy.

results.result: osl-dynamics is presented as a Python-based open-source toolbox that uses machine learning generative models to identify and describe recurrent brain dynamics on fast timescales (tens of milliseconds) across multiple neuroimaging modalities including MEG, fMRI, LFP, and ECoG.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 describe the toolbox's core capabilities and are supported by the demonstrated applications throughout the manuscript. Claims C47-C49 regarding Python implementation and its advantages are explicitly stated and justified. The multi-modality applicability (C3) is supported by citations to prior work using these methods.

results.result: The TDE-HMM can identify oscillatory bursts in a data-driven manner without pre-specifying frequency, amplitude threshold, or duration, detecting bursts with lifetimes ranging from hundreds of milliseconds and automatically identifying oscillation frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C12 and C14 are directly supported by the burst detection results shown in Figure 1, where the TDE-HMM identifies three states with distinct spectral properties and varying lifetimes. Claims C40-C41 regarding advantages over conventional methods are stated and conceptually sound, though direct comparative validation is not shown in this manuscript.

results.result: The AE-HMM identifies plausible functional networks (default mode, visual, frontotemporal, sensorimotor) with fast dynamics (~50 ms lifetimes) and detects significant task-related activations of visual networks (50-100 ms post-stimulus, p<0.05) and frontotemporal networks (300-900 ms post-stimulus, p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 are supported by Figure 2A showing identified networks and their dynamics. Claims C17-C18 regarding task-related activations are supported by Figure 2B with appropriate statistical testing (p<0.05) and permutation testing to control family-wise error rate. The networks are validated as plausible by citation to Buckner et al., 2011.

results.result: The TDE-HMM identifies networks with distinct spectral characteristics and fast dynamics (~50 ms lifetimes), showing spatial patterns consistent with AE-HMM results and similar networks across rest and task conditions, with high power regions showing high coherence.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 are supported by Figure 3 showing state-specific PSDs, power maps, and lifetime distributions. Claim C20 is validated by visual comparison between Figures 2 and 3. Claim C22 is supported by comparison of Figures 3 and 4 with citation to Smith et al., 2009. Claim C23 is supported by coherence networks shown in Figures 3AI and 4AI.

results.result: In the CTF rest dataset, older participants (34-60 years) show significantly increased fractional occupancy and switching rate of the sensorimotor network (p<0.05), decreased mean lifetime of the visual network (p<0.05), and wider distribution of mean intervals for default mode and suppressed states (p<0.05) compared to younger participants (18-34 years).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are all supported by Figure 4BI with appropriate statistical testing (p<0.05) and permutation testing controlling for family-wise error rate. The authors appropriately note (C67) that these findings are consistent with existing studies (Coquelet et al., 2020) and acknowledge this is an illustrative example requiring more rigorous future study.

results.result: DyNeMo identifies more localized power activations and cleaner network structure than TDE-HMM, with networks showing distinct spectral characteristics and overlapping dynamics. In the age comparison, DyNeMo reveals stronger effect sizes (p<0.01) for sensorimotor network differences and identifies decreased variability in the left temporal network (p<0.01) in older participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 are supported by Figure 5A showing DyNeMo's network identification and mode correlations. Claims C32-C33 regarding age-related differences are supported by Figure 5BI with appropriate statistical testing. The comparison showing DyNeMo's stronger effect size (p<0.01 vs p<0.05 for HMM) is explicitly demonstrated, though the authors appropriately note this is task-dependent (C73).

results.result: The TDE-HMM models dynamics in both oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization (unlike AE-HMM which only models amplitude), while HMM assumes mutually exclusive states and DyNeMo assumes mixed modes, providing complementary descriptions of network dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 accurately describe fundamental differences between the methods as stated in the manuscript and supported by the mathematical formulations in Figure 7. Claims C71-C72 regarding complementary nature are appropriately stated as interpretive conclusions supported by citation to Gohil et al., 2022 and demonstrated through the different perspectives shown in the results.

results.result: DyNeMo uses richer temporal regularization through a deep recurrent network compared to HMM, which has been shown to capture longer-range temporal structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by citation to Gohil et al., 2022 and are consistent with the architectural differences shown in Figure 7B. The claim is appropriately attributed to prior validation work rather than being demonstrated de novo in this manuscript.

results.result: The sliding window approach for calculating time series properties suffers from a tradeoff between temporal precision and accurate estimation and is inadequate for studying fast changes in functional connectivity, while generative models can identify non-contiguous segments sharing the same latent variable for more robust estimates.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 accurately describes a known limitation of sliding window approaches. Claim C51 is supported by citation to Liuzzi et al., 2019. Claim C52 describes the theoretical advantage of the generative model approach, which is conceptually sound and consistent with the methodology presented.

results.result: The HMM uses variational Bayesian inference to learn latent states with the advantage of accounting for uncertainty, while DyNeMo uses amortized variational Bayesian inference to overcome HMM limitations (mutually exclusive states and limited memory), providing a highly efficient and scalable inference scheme.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 regarding HMM are supported by citations to Bishop and Nasrabadi, 2006 and multiple application papers. Claims C56-C58 regarding DyNeMo are supported by citations to Gohil et al., 2022 and Kingma and Welling, 2013. The mathematical formulations in Figure 7 support these methodological descriptions.

results.result: Time-delay embedding augments time series with time-lagged channels, embedding the autocorrelation function into the covariance matrix, making it sensitive to oscillation frequency and enabling study of dynamics in both oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 accurately describe the TDE methodology and are supported by the illustration in Figure 9C. The mathematical relationship between TDE and spectral properties is correctly stated and demonstrated visually.

results.result: HMM and DyNeMo are trained by minimizing variational free energy but suffer from local optimum issues leading to run-to-run variability. The strategy of training 10 models and selecting the best run consistently finds the same model parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 accurately describe the training procedure and its limitations. Claim C65 describes the mitigation strategy used. Claim C66 is supported by the reproducibility analysis shown in supplementary figures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 through Figure 5—figure supplement 1), demonstrating consistent results across independent sets of runs.

results.result: Both HMM and DyNeMo have been validated on simulated data for burst detection and dynamic network identification applications.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by citations to Quinn et al., 2019 for HMM burst detection validation and Vidaurre et al., 2016; Gohil et al., 2022 for dynamic network validation. While the validation is not shown in this manuscript, the citations to prior validation work are appropriate.

results.result: The observed age-related differences are consistent with existing studies, and static power differences can arise from either more frequent network activations or altered power within networks while dynamics remain unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 is supported by citation to Coquelet et al., 2020. However, claims C69-C70 are explicitly stated as speculative explanations ("could be due to", "may arise from") without direct validation. The authors appropriately acknowledge these are possible interpretations requiring further investigation, but the mechanistic claims remain unvalidated hypotheses.

results.result: Better performance in downstream tasks indicates a more useful model, and osl-dynamics can compute static network descriptions using the same methodology as dynamic approaches for straightforward comparisons.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 presents a reasonable criterion for model evaluation, though it is stated as an argument rather than an established principle. Claim C74 is supported by the demonstration in Section 2.5 and Figure 6 showing static network analysis using consistent methodology.

results.result: The manuscript describes various methodological details including burst detection assumptions, spectral estimation approaches, dimensionality reduction needs, network thresholding methods, and DyNeMo-specific complications regarding mode time course interpretation and renormalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C87 describe methodological details and implementation choices. These are appropriately documented with citations where applicable (e.g., C79 to Vidaurre et al., 2016; C81 to Vidaurre et al., 2018b; C82 to Quinn et al., 2022a and Gohil et al., 2022; C84-C85 to Gohil et al., 2022). The methods are clearly stated and justified.

results.result: Different state/mode time courses can lead to similar variational free energy values due to local optima, with sensitivity to stochasticity and initial values. Reproducibility is defined as consistently inferring the same model parameters, with only relative differences in free energy being important for a given set of hyperparameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 accurately describe characteristics of the training process and reproducibility criteria. These are standard considerations in variational inference and are appropriately documented. The reproducibility analysis in supplementary figures supports these statements.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior work establishing that neural oscillations are linked to cognitive processes, communication, and disease, with recent evidence for short oscillatory bursts (~100 ms) occurring across cortical networks and network dynamics being predictive of behavioral traits and disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C11 are all appropriately supported by citations to prior work (Ward, 2003; Fries, 2015; Başar and Güntekin, 2008; Jones, 2016; Shin et al., 2017; Seedat et al., 2020; Vidaurre et al., 2018b; Quinn et al., 2018; Higgins et al., 2021; Liégeois et al., 2019; Sitnikova et al., 2018; Du et al., 2018; Van Schependom et al., 2019; Salvan et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2020). These claims accurately represent the cited literature and provide appropriate context.

results.result: The authors present osl-dynamics, a Python-based toolbox that uses machine learning generative models to identify and describe recurrent brain dynamics on fast timescales (tens of milliseconds) across multiple neuroimaging modalities. The toolbox is open-source, avoids paid licenses, and leverages modern deep learning libraries like TensorFlow for scalability.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm the toolbox's utility and comprehensive nature. Reviewer 1 states 'The utility of the toolbox is compelling and demonstrated through a series of exemplar brain imaging datasets' and calls it 'fundamental work.' Reviewer 3 notes 'This toolbox will be a great asset to the brain imaging community.' No concerns were raised about the core capabilities or implementation.

results.result: The TDE-HMM can identify oscillatory bursts in a data-driven fashion without pre-specifying frequency, amplitude threshold, or duration. The identified bursts have lifetimes ranging from hundreds of milliseconds and the method is less sensitive to amplitude than conventional thresholding approaches.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises concerns about validation, stating 'it would be very interesting to test whether this method can "keep up" as the data is made more challenging' with synthetic data. They note that 'showing results from brain signals directly (e.g., Figure 7) is nice, it will be even more impactful if it is backed up with results obtained from synthetic data with known properties.' While the authors note concerns were 'addressed' in revision, the original concern about synthetic validation remains documented.

results.result: The AE-HMM identifies plausible functional networks (default mode, visual, frontotemporal, sensorimotor) with fast dynamics (~50 ms lifetimes). In task data, visual networks show significant activation 50-100 ms after visual stimuli, and a frontotemporal network activates 300-900 ms post-stimulus.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes the methods are 'well described and demonstrated within multiple peer reviewed articles.' Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'We see similarities between states across multiple runs (reproducibility analysis) and across tasks (e.g. Figure 8 vs 9) and even methods (Figure 8 vs 10), which is great.' The task-evoked responses align with expected timing.

results.result: The TDE-HMM identifies networks with distinct spectral activity and fast dynamics (~50 ms lifetimes). Power maps show similar spatial patterns to AE-HMM amplitude maps, regions with high power show high coherence, and similar networks are observed in rest and task data.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'We see similarities between states across multiple runs (reproducibility analysis) and across tasks (e.g. Figure 8 vs 9) and even methods (Figure 8 vs 10), which is great,' confirming the consistency across methods and conditions. The rest-task similarity is supported by citation to fMRI literature.

results.result: Age-related differences show increased fractional occupancy and switching rate of the sensorimotor network, decreased mean lifetime of the visual network, and wider distribution of mean intervals for default mode and suppressed states in older participants (34-60 years) compared to younger (18-34 years). These findings are consistent with existing studies.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically requests clarification: 'the comparison across subjects is interesting, but it is not clear why sensory-motor areas show a difference and the mean lifetime of the visual network decreases. Can you please explain this better? The promised discussion in section 3.5 can be expanded as well.' While the authors cite consistency with Coquelet et al. 2020, the reviewer indicates the mechanistic interpretation needs strengthening.

results.result: DyNeMo identifies more localized power activations and cleaner network structure than TDE-HMM, with distinct spectral characteristics and overlapping networks that vary in mixing ratios. DyNeMo reveals stronger effect sizes (p<0.01 vs p<0.05) for age-related differences in sensorimotor network contribution and decreased variability in left temporal network in older participants.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings. Reviewer 2 notes the consistency 'across tasks (e.g. Figure 8 vs 9) and even methods (Figure 8 vs 10), which is great.' Reviewer 3 states 'The only question I had (originally) was how to objectively/quantitatively compare different network models. This has now been addressed by the authors in the latest revision,' indicating acceptance of the comparative claims.

results.result: The TDE-HMM models dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization while AE-HMM models only amplitude. HMM assumes mutually exclusive states while DyNeMo assumes mixed modes. DyNeMo uses richer temporal regularization and captures longer-range temporal structure, but HMM's stronger assumptions simplify interpretation. The methods provide complementary descriptions, with better downstream task performance indicating a more useful model.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly confirms 'The only question I had (originally) was how to objectively/quantitatively compare different network models. This has now been addressed by the authors in the latest revision.' This indicates acceptance of the comparative framework and the complementary nature of the methods. No reviewer challenges the methodological distinctions.

results.result: The sliding window approach suffers from a tradeoff between temporal precision and accurate estimation and is inadequate for studying fast changes in functional connectivity. Generative models overcome this by identifying non-contiguous segments sharing the same latent variable, leading to more robust estimates.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this methodological rationale. Reviewer 3 affirms 'The methods described are principled, based on generative probabilistic models. This makes them compact descriptors of the complex time-frequency data. Few initial assumptions are necessary.' The citation to Liuzzi et al. 2019 supports the inadequacy claim.

results.result: The HMM uses variational Bayesian inference to account for uncertainty in latent states and has been successfully used in various neuroimaging settings. DyNeMo overcomes HMM limitations using amortized variational Bayesian inference, which is highly efficient and scalable to large datasets.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'The methods described are principled, based on generative probabilistic models' and 'The methods are well described and demonstrated within multiple peer reviewed articles.' The extensive citations support the successful application claims. No reviewer challenges the inference methodology.

results.result: Time-delay embedding augments time series with time-lagged channels, embedding the autocorrelation function into the covariance matrix. This makes the covariance sensitive to oscillation frequency and allows study of dynamics in oscillatory amplitude and phase synchronization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the TDE methodology. Reviewer 3 notes 'Few initial assumptions are necessary in order to reveal this compact description,' which aligns with the data-driven nature of TDE. The technical description is accepted without critique.

results.result: HMM and DyNeMo are trained by minimizing variational free energy but suffer from local optimum issues leading to run-to-run variability. The strategy of training multiple models and selecting the best run (lowest free energy) from a set of 10 consistently finds the same model parameters, establishing reproducibility.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 initially requested 'The authors should explain the reproducibility results (variational free energy and best run analysis) in the Results section itself, to better orient the reader on what to look for.' The revised manuscript addresses this, and Reviewer 2 confirms 'the authors have addressed all the concerns raised earlier.' The reproducibility approach is accepted.

results.result: Static differences in power between age groups can arise from multiple dynamic mechanisms: more frequent network activations or altered power within networks while dynamics remain unchanged.
results.evaluation: These are presented as interpretive possibilities rather than definitive claims. Reviewer 2's request for better explanation of age differences suggests these interpretations are reasonable but could be expanded. No reviewer challenges the logic of these alternative explanations.

results.result: osl-dynamics can compute static network descriptions using the same methodology as dynamic approaches, facilitating comparisons. Both HMM and DyNeMo have been validated on simulated data for burst detection and dynamic network identification.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes the importance of synthetic validation but acknowledges existing validation work through citations (Quinn et al. 2019; Vidaurre et al. 2016; Gohil et al. 2022). While requesting additional synthetic validation for the specific applications shown, the reviewer accepts that validation has been performed in prior work.

results.result: Neural oscillations are linked to cognitive processes, communication, and disease. Recent evidence suggests neuronal populations exhibit short bursts of oscillatory activity (~100 ms) across cortical networks, with network dynamics linked to memory replay, behavioral traits, and disease prediction.
results.evaluation: These background claims are well-cited and not challenged by any reviewer. They provide established context for the toolbox's purpose. Reviewers focus their evaluation on the novel methodological contributions rather than questioning the motivating neuroscience literature.

results.result: Technical implementation details including single-channel burst detection assumptions, multitaper spectral estimation, PCA dimensionality reduction after TDE, non-negative matrix factorization for frequency band identification, GLM-based PSD calculation in DyNeMo, mode time course renormalization, GMM-based binarization and thresholding approaches.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'The methods described are principled, based on generative probabilistic models' and 'The methods are well described and demonstrated within multiple peer reviewed articles.' These technical details are presented with appropriate citations and are not challenged by reviewers.
